newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Sorghum planting down in Queensland Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Sorghum planting down in Queensland Australia.

text.p: With sorghum planting still taking place in Australia's central Queensland, it is clear the area will be lower than for last year's bumper crop, grain cooperative Grainco said in its weekly market review.
Only limited tonnages of new crop sorghum traded over the past week as winter harvest progressed and consumers watched for feed wheat opportunities, trading manager Rob Brealey said.
This occurred as futures markets drifted lower, he said.
With both domestic and international markets in feed barley in a quiet buying period, the value of feed barley eased over the past week.
Pressure continued to build from increasing world stocks of feed grains, particularly from North America where feed wheat, feed barley and corn stocks were plentiful, Brealey said.
The European Union's decision not to increase the export subsidy for feed barley was felt likely to not last for long.
The higher the export subsidy from Europe, the more bearish the view for international values, he said.
Domestically in Australia, growers and buyers were reluctant participants at current levels. Domestic feed barley values may be close to the bottom, he said.

International malting barley values were reasonably stable as importing countries, particularly China, looked to Australia for projected production levels and anticipated export tonnages. International demand remained relatively strong, he said.
Of growing concern to international buyers was the large price differential between feed and malt barley values.
Domestically, values were firmer over the past week.

Increased inquiries from the export market for cottonseed emerged in the past week from November 1996 to March 1997. The Japanese market in particular had a reasonable amount of coverage to effect before availability of new crop.
Export market prices had not improved appreciably but an increasing number of trading houses were realising that Australian supply was becoming tight, he said.
In pulses, harvest of desi type chickpea in central Queensland was almost complete, with only about half of expected production realised mainly because of frost and rain damage.
In some cases crops remain unharvested as it was not economic to take remaining seed off, he said.
An estimated 15 percent of the central Queensland crop was lost because of splitting after rains.
With southern Queensland another two weeks away from the general chickpea harvest, crops looked promising, he said.
Prices remained soft as export markets weakened.
Domestic oilseed values declined last week with new crop black sunflowers finishing the week at A$335 a tonne delivered Brisbane.
New crop soybean prices fell A$5.00 a tonne to A$385.00 a tonne delivered Brisbane, while canola prices were also down, to A$340.00 a tonne Moree for November/December delivery.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
